title: Largest population the results apply to
subtitle: Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments  · 5 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **5 of the official questions in Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments  are this one** — 0 Easy, 1 Medium, 4 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The stem ends by asking for the largest population or group the results can be generalized or applied to.
- The four choices are populations nested inside each other, from 'only the people in the sample' out to much broader groups.
- Sometimes a table is shown that includes only part of the sample, such as members who met some minimum threshold.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Find the exact group the sample was randomly drawn from, with every qualifier: the place, the age or level, the subgroup, and any minimum threshold stated for the data shown.
- 2) Pick the choice that matches that group exactly, keeping every qualifier.
- 3) If the subjects were randomly assigned to treatments but not randomly selected from a larger group, the results reach only as far as the group they were actually drawn from.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You pick a broader group, such as the whole region, all ages or everyone in the category, because it sounds more impressive.
Or you pick the narrowest choice (only the sample) because you think a sample can never speak for anything larger.
You also drop a qualifier, such as the threshold that defines which members appear in the table.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You pick a broader group, such as the whole region, all ages or everyone in the category, because it sounds more impressive.
Or you pick the narrowest choice (only the sample) because you think a sample can never speak for anything larger.
